utterances.text: No. No, I don't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: So there's nothing in there about Milan Simic firing at least two shots in your 1998 statement; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this statement, it is not to be found.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Okay. In this statement or in your 1995 statement. We'll talk about both of that, then -- those, then.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: So nowhere in your 1998 statement or your 1995 statement that you read here today is there anything about all these details - bullets passing between you and your brother, glass shattering, gun waving, gun pointing and firing shots - yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these statements, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: So therefore, after nine years, these details now come to your memory and come before the Tribunal, after nine years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, you gave the statement that's in front of you in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could we actually have this marked, Your Honour, because we have been discussing it, and it should be marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought it was. Yes. Let me find out from the Registry assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The 1998 statement was marked, not the 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The 1998 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be marked Defence Exhibit D7/2 ter and D7/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe to complete the whole thing about these statements, it will be better to have them both on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's the 1998. I believe the 1995 statement has already been marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is already -- Yes. Okay. The 1998 one then should also be on record. Yes. Can we have the number? I'm wondering whether we have --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I already -- I just gave the number, I thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- as exhibits now, the same numbers, for both statements, 1995 and 1998, the English and the Serbo-Croat versions. We have the numbers already?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes. Re-examination can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, you gave this statement in 1998? Could you speak louder, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was this statement voluntary?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did anyone influence any of the statements that you made to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you what to say in that statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How come, Mr. Bicic, that you're able to testify to certain facts now that you didn't place in your previous statements?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, as I made several statements, the first time it was terrible to live through it all once again, so that at those moving moments, as I was talking, I probably left a lot out. And also in my second statement, the same occurred. However, when I was given the statements here to review them and read them, I saw that I had left out some things which I had remembered, and then I added them, referring to them here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your testimony here, has it been truthful?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a couple questions about the lawsuit in the United States. Who initiated that lawsuit?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The complaint was filed by Kemal Mesinovic, who is living in the United States, having recognised Vukovic in the street. I don't know where. Then he called me up and some other people that he knew had been beaten by that same man. I responded to his request to be a witness, without knowing that I too would become a plaintiff, to confirm that Nikola Vukovic had, using false identification documents, been admitted to the United States of America as an immigrant. Actually, he forged some documents and registered there as Nikola Nikolic. I knew him because his wife had, several years before this pizzeria of ours was renovated and refurbished - it used to be a restaurant - she had worked for me for a couple of years. I said five or six years. I can't remember exactly. She was an assistant cook. Also, his sister used to live across the street from this establishment of ours, and then I would see Vukovic very frequently passing by. So Kemal asked me to testify and to identify him and to testify about all the things that this man did in the camp under the nickname Miki.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you obtain the attorney in this case?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I never saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who initiated the case and when to see the attorney, you or Kemal?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kemal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, during the cross-examination you were shown a document about some sort of hunters' group, where you were listed in the reserve, some sort of alleged document of TO or SDA members, and counsel asked if you knew who these individuals were, and you indicated that you did. And then counsel asked: Do you know whether or not these are SDA members? And you said no, you did not. Were you a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you attend on a regular basis, or any sort of basis, SDA meetings?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have any involvement with the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you have any interest in politics in general, any of the political parties?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the last area I'd like to discuss is - D9/4 is the English, and D9/4 ter in B/C/S - the document of Simo Zaric's interrogation at Brcko. Could the usher please show the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to look at the first page, and I'd invite your attention to the second paragraph, the second sentence of the second paragraph. Do you see where it says "We waited until two unidentified individuals in camouflage uniforms came"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, this is quite illegible. I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll read the sentence, and I'll ask you to comment on it. It's in the English version, the second paragraph, which would be D9.4. "We waited until two unidentified individuals in camouflage uniforms came, and we handed them all the weapons. At their request, we got into the Golf -- into a Golf, and drove to the SJB, Public Security Station, and from there, we were taken to prison at the SUP." Could you find that in your B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought the witness said the copy he has is illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me just ask you this, sir: Is that true? Is that a correct statement, with regard to the section "At their request, we got into the Golf -- into a Golf"? Is that portion of the statement true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that we got into the Golf at their request. We were thrown into it. They were beating us. They simply threw us into that Golf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to invite your attention to the next page, the statement, page 2 in the English, top paragraph. It's not the full paragraph. The top paragraph, first full sentence on that page: "As far as I know, Alija Fitozovic was a man who acted on behalf of the SDA, and members of the SDA were illegally armed through him." Specifically, I'm referring to the phrase "were illegally armed through him." Do you recall ever making that statement to Simo Zaric during the interrogation at Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I made a statement, but under what conditions ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever use the phrase that Fitozovic was illegally arming members of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, sir. That completes redirect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I have one question, Mr. Bicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac where you were living, you explained you had business enterprises which you were running. Were there Serbs with similar business enterprises?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not enterprises, really. These were shops, catering establishments, and other people also owned catering establishments, restaurants, privately owned shops, things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to find out whether those others who owned similar establishments were also detained with you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean persons who were ethnic Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not detained with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: As far as you know, did they remain running their enterprises, after you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really say, but I heard from the guards that they were in some catering establishments that were run by ethnic Serbs. I heard what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What were they saying?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they talked, amongst themselves, that they went for a drink to Neven Markovic's. He had a cafe in an industrial neighbourhood, in a neighbourhood in the industrial zone, perhaps I could put it that way, an industrial zone of Bosanski Samac. And also to Misa Sekin. That's what he was called. And some other people, to Ignjo, people like that, people who ran cafes, catering establishments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, if I might just ask one or two questions. Firstly, in connection with the civil suit in America, for what it's worth, did you ever give or submit a statement personally to any lawyer in the United States?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A gentleman came to see me at my home. Now, I don't know whether he's a lawyer, because I don't speak English. He briefly jotted something down. And then a few months later, I was asked to come to Ulm, to a university there, and I talked there, again with a man who lectured at that university, who came from the United States. But at that time, my German was not that good, so we tried to communicate but not in a very meaningful way, without much accuracy. How should I put this? Oh, yes. There was a lady there, too, who was working there, but I don't think she was a certified interpreter. She was simply helping with the translation. She spoke our language. So officially, I did not meet with lawyers except for these people. And these people came from some organisation. I can't remember exactly what the name of this organisation was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: All right. But you did not send in a signed statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, I did not. We just talked about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: The second question is: When you moved from the secondary school to the primary school, that is, after two days of detention there, did all the detainees move? Because, I think, on the second night, some more detainees came in. Did they all move to the primary school, or did some remain back in the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we were all transferred to the primary school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I just have one small question, Mr. Bicic. This also concerns the civil suit in the U.S. I wonder whether you could recall approximately the date when you gave this statement or interview with the American professor at Ulm? The reason I'm asking that is I'm wondering whether it was before or after this Statement of Claim in the civil suit was filed. I hope the question is clear. If it's not, I'll make it shorter.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- well, I know that it was wintertime; that, I know for sure. It was three or four years ago. I can't tell you the exact date, really. I know that a friend gave me a ride and that it was snowing heavily, so we were considerably delayed. We came much later than we were supposed to come. We agreed to meet at that university between 9.00 and 10.00; however, we arrived only after 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And just to clarify, was that after you gave the 1998 statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, the unsigned one that we looked at?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not really answer this question with any certainty. I really don't know. For me, it was something unofficial. We just talked about this. He asked me about what was going on and what had happened, and he brought his picture, this man's picture, and he brought a few pictures. And I said, "Yes, that's the man. His name is Vukovic, not Nikolic," and we talked a little bit. As I said, we talked a little bit, until this lady came who spoke a bit of our language, and then she tried to interpret. This gentleman spoke German much better than I did. So I'm not sure whether it was before my statement or after it. I really can't say that for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any questions arising from the questions from the -- the answers from the questions from the Bench? Any questions? Yes, the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Bicic, for giving evidence to the Tribunal. You are now free. You can go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. [The witness withdrew].

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour? Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: May I just take advantage of this pause in the proceedings just to put on the record that in complying with your request on the memorandum of the witnesses with whom Mr. Pisarevic may potentially have a conflict, whether that be perceived or real, we did file that with the Registry today, just before this witness would take the stand, and I gave a copy of that to the Defence, although, of course, they will get an official copy when it's filed with the Registry. And although the witness and Mr. -- the following witness and Mr. Pisarevic have had some contact, we don't believe that there is any potential -- I mean, there's no reason that Mr. Pisarevic himself, should he choose not to conduct the cross-examination. But just so you're advised that we have complied with your request to provide that memorandum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Where is the next witness? Mr. Usher, is there a witness? Oh, I see. He needed to be told as he was leaving that he should come back with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please make the solemn declaration while standing, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes. I'll get up, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, my hearing is not very good, so could the volume in these headphones be turned up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The usher can assist with that. Because the usher has no earphones, so -- he wants more volume. Yes. Perhaps the interpreter can greet the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear even less now. Even less. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The greeting again to test the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very poorly. I can hardly hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe we -- maybe we change the earphones. MR. DI FAZIO: Testing, testing, testing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We have a spare set.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So you can sit down now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. di Fazio, you can proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, on the question of your hearing, I want you to make sure during your testimony that if you haven't heard a question, either from myself or from Defence counsel or from the Bench, would you make that clear rather than answering to something that you think has been asked you. Make sure you're always clear about the question that's being put to you. Okay?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How old are they?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: My son is 21, and my daughter is 13.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think he can be assisted to push the chair towards the desk. MR. DI FAZIO: And could I -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: I was born in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where do you currently live?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: I currently live 6 kilometres away from Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is that in Republika Srpska or the Federation part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's in the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You said that you were born in Bosanski Samac. Where did you live up until April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you married whilst living in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you were born there. What about your ancestors? By that, I mean going back a couple of generations - your grandfather, great-grandfather, and so on - where did they live?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes. They all lived there. They were born there. As a matter of fact, they were among the first people to come to Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What ethnic background are you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: I am a Muslim. I'm sorry. I meant ethnic Bosniak, and by religion, I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, did you perform military service?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Ask you remember where that was?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did my military service in Pula and in Split, from the 27th of September, 1973, and then I got out on the 21st of March, 1975, because my military service went on for 18 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you specialise in any particular aspect of military matters, military activity?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: It was a navy unit that was a mine -- an anti-mine unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: As a young man, were you a sportsman?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever engage in canoeing as a sport?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What sort of level did you get to in that particular sport?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: I was, in fact, champion of Yugoslavia, so it was a very high level.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you compete on an international level?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: I did. I even took part as a member of the Yugoslav national team.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What years were you on the Yugoslavian national team?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1970 until 1973, when I went to do my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Prior to April of 1992, we've heard evidence that the basic population layout in the municipality of Bosanski Samac was this: Most of the Muslims lived in the town of Bosanski Samac, Croats lived in Croat villages surrounding the town of Bosanski Samac, and Serbs lived in Serb villages also surrounding the town of Bosanski Samac, and furthermore, members of all three ethnic groups lived mixed and interspersed in the town of Bosanski Samac. Would you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was your occupation, what sort of work did you do, in the years leading up to April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: I had my own crafts shop, which principally provided metalwork, metal sheetings for buildings, for construction work. I had my own private business, water pipes and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was it the case that if someone building something, construction site, for example, needed parts or metal parts, they would come to you so that you could fashion and make the parts necessary?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite right. It was a combined locksmiths and tinsmiths, so I manufactured steel doors and windows with aluminium covers. So my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the period of time leading up to April of 1992, was your wife engaged in any sort of business?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What did she do?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: She was working in the primary school. She was a supplier, somebody who carried the mail. This was until about six months before the war. And then I opened for her a business with video games, and she was supposed to devote herself full time to that, to video games.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was that business, the video game business, up and running as at April 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If I may just return briefly to your sporting activities. Apart from canoeing, did you hunt and fish?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I also played handball. I was a member of the city team for handball for many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm more interested in the hunting and fishing. Did you possess weapons in order for you to carry out your hunting activities?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had two hunting rifles: we called it a Sacmarica, and a hunting carbine for large game.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of any hunting clubs or organisations?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the hunting society called Fazan, or Pheasant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is that strictly a Bosanski Samac club, or is that something that is Bosnia-wide or indeed Yugoslavia-wide?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: No. This society covered only the territory of Bosanski Samac municipality. That is the town and the surrounding villages that came within the same municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long had it been in existence and carrying on its activities as at April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: I'm not able to tell you exactly when it was started, but I am 48 years old, and as a small child of five or six, I had already started hunting, so it existed and I have been a member since 1975. That is when I came back from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did it have headquarters, a club room, something like that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were two rooms. One was in town itself, a kind of office where you could pay your membership fees and a secretary was there to take care of daily affairs. And there was a facility in the village of Donja Slatina, and it was called the Hunting Lodge or Hunting Club.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: May I just seek a clarification there? Where is Donja Slatina and how often were you and the others away on hunting trips?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Donja Slatina is about 10 to 12 kilometres away from the town of Samac, and we would go hunting there quite often. It would be on Sundays during the hunting season, and the hunting season started depending on the kind of game that one was hunting, whether it was large game or small game.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If I could just ask you, Mr. Salkic, a follow-up question. Was this village of Donja Slatina an ethnic Serb or an ethnic Croat village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Donja Slatina is a Serb village, Donja Slatina. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did Fazan, or Pheasant, ever organise hunting trips for its members?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The organisation of the hunting society Fazan consisted of several sections, so there may have been two or three villages in one section, then Samac, the whole town, in another section. And then within those sections themselves, there were groups, groups of hunters which had to consist of at least five hunters, but the maximum was unlimited. So it was rarely that Fazan organised hunting for us. But we had some members working abroad, so we would organise a couple of days before New Year's Day or just after New Year's Day for those people who did not have occasion to join us in our hunting trips regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: We've referred to three ethnic groups in the -- living in the area, the Croats, Serbs, and Muslims. Were members of all those three groups represented in Fazan?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I want to ask you now if you've ever been a member of a political party.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: No, no, until a year prior to the war, when I joined the SDA political party, which I abandoned six months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Firstly, let's go to the issue of your joining the SDA. Why did you join it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: I joined the SDA like anyone who had a position of his own. I liked the programme of this party and, like any other citizen, it was my democratic right to join one of the political parties, and I decided that it should be the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you say that you were a member for some months and then decided to abandon it, how did you abandon it? Did you actually do something to abandon it or did you just cease actively participating or doing anything on behalf of the party?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: I never had any official position in the party, so I couldn't withdraw from those activities. I was just an ordinary member with a membership card, and the way I had picked it up when I joined, I returned it. I went to the party office, said I didn't want to be a member any more, and handed my card back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: During the period of time that you were a member, did you ever engage in any sort of party activities? I don't necessarily mean holding position, but did you do anything, fund-raising, going to meetings, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I don't want to put words in your mouth, but you tell me if this is a correct scenario: You joined, paid your membership, and that was the extent of it. Now, is that correct, or did you engage in more -- more activities?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: The former is correct. I paid my membership fees, I was a member, and I simply abandoned it. I wasn't involved in anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: I've known him for quite a long time, since my early youth. That would make it about 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever socialise with him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Not really, but we would always greet one another in the street, because he was a doctor. When we were young, we would just say hello, but later on he was a doctor, and I would always address him with respect, as "the doctor."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was he a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: I cannot say that he was, but I do know that -- I don't know how I can explain it, but I heard from others that he was in the SDS. People were saying this. I never saw his membership card, so I can't claim that he actually belonged to that political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Have a look around the courtroom. If you see him, point him out.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: This gentleman over there with a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Also for a long time, 25 to 30 years, maybe even longer, but something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We called him Miro, and also Brko, Mustacio [phoen], because he almost always wore a moustache, and so we called him Brko.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of an establishment called Cafe AS, A-S?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was he connected in any way with that establishment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think he was the owner. If it wasn't he, then it was his wife or his son, but I think it was Mr. Miroslav who was the owner.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever go to that place, that cafe?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the period of -- I'll withdraw that. In the period of time leading up to April of 1992, did you go to the Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, until perhaps the last two and a half to three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was there any reason for your ceasing to go in the last two and a half to three months?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: The reason was that I experienced some unpleasantness there from some people, and later on I was to see that they were people from the 4th Detachment. They told me that that was not my place there, and then Mr. Miro's son got up and said that I was a guest there and that I should be left alone. And after that I really thought myself that maybe I shouldn't go there any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So a member of Mr. Tadic's family was polite to you and informed you that you were still welcome; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you look around the courtroom, and if you see Mr. Tadic, point him out, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: There he is. I'm sure he won't take it against me if I say he has a moustache when I point at him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about Milan Simic? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: I've known him also for a long time. We lived together in the same town. Again, some 25 to 30 years, and more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever socialise with him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Occasionally we'd meet at a cafe here and there. One might say we were on good terms. Because Samac was a small town. Everyone knew everyone else. It's not a big city. We did socialise, and sometimes if I needed something, he would do me a favour too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What sort of favours?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: For instance, I didn't have a fax machine. Then I would go to his company. Mr. Predrag Blagojevic worked [Realtime transcript read in error "lived"] with him, and I knew him very well. I used to play handball with him. And we'd have a cup of coffee, and in the meantime my fax would be sent. And we'd have a chat, and we were really on good terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you know his family?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. There is a problem with the transcript. The witness has said that Mr. Predrag Blagojevic worked with him and it says here "lived with him." Could you please -- I mean, if my colleague can testify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- clarify that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecutor can clarify that with the witness. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just a little clarification, Mr. Salkic. The transcript says that Mr. Predrag Blagojevic lived with Milan Simic. Did you mean to say that he worked with --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: No, no. They worked together in the same company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, there's been evidence in the case that you know Muhamed Bicic and Hasan Bicic and are friends with those two men. Can you tell us if Milan Simic was apparently friendly with those two men?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes. They would often meet in the establishment that the Bicics had. They would meet and talk. In fact, I think they were on better terms with him than I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Perica Misic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What ethnic background is he?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: A Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you inform the Chamber if Milan Simic knew or was friendly with Perica Misic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, I can confirm that they knew each other. I think they worked together even. As to whether they were really friends, I am unable to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Look around the courtroom. If you see Milan Simic, point him out, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see him, over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And Mr. Simo Zaric, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Also as long as the others. For a long, long time we've known each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Would you greet each other in the street prior to April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we would greet each other. We went hunting together. Sometimes we would organise something, sit together, have a drink together, yes. For many years we went hunting together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you went hunting together, were these hunting trips when Mr. Simo Zaric was present conducted under the auspices or the umbrella or organised by Fazan?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, because this was a regular hunt. You couldn't otherwise go to the hunting grounds. For a time, in fact, we were in the same hunting group. As I was explaining a moment ago, the group has to have at least five members, upwards, and there were at least 15 of us in this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Have a look around this room and see if you can point him out.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there he is, wearing glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who is on his left?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And on the right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagoje Simic. MR. DI FAZIO: And if Your Honours please, may the transcript reflect that he's correctly identified all the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask you some more questions about another individual, Fadil Topcagic. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What ethnic background is he?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Since my early childhood, since when I was five or six. I know him for as long as I have known myself more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: For the record, you might want to go back to line 108.20 where you said that the witness has correctly identified all the witnesses. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry, I'm grateful to Your Honour for that. Yes. Perhaps the record should -- or rather the transcript should indicate that the witness has correctly identified the defendants in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just a few more questions before 5.00, Mr. Salkic. Is Topcagic related to Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: No. He's not a relative of his. Fadil's sister is Mr. Simo Zaric's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So he's his brother-in-law?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: We call it surjak, sister's husband. In Bosnia, we call that surjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Were they apparently friendly?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, normally, as relations, but they were on good terms anyway. Both of them hunted with me, and I think they were on good terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the period of time, in the months leading up to April of 1992, did you go on any hunting trips with Fadil Topcagic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long before the 16th of April, 1992 was the last hunting trip that you went on with Fadil Topcagic? If you don't know exactly, give us an approximation.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, there's three and a half months in the new year and a month before that, so about four and a half months. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I'm going to move on to another topic. We've only got a minute left. Could we break now and keep the continuity going?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn and continue tomorrow at 0930 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
